claims.text: Inducing stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy will increase its radiation tolerance.
The SCCP treatment will reduce radiation-induced defect clusters and voids relative to the untreated alloy.
SCCPs can preserve or enhance the strength and tensile ductility of a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
A solution heat treatment followed by controlled aging at approximately 800°C will induce SCCPs.
Solution heat treatment will homogenize the alloy structure.
Controlled aging near 800°C can produce stable coherent nanoprecipitates without excessive coarsening.
The treatment will produce coherent nanoprecipitates uniformly distributed within the HEA matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
The coherent interfaces enhance recombination of radiation-induced defects.
Coherent SCCP interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and help prevent stress concentrations and premature cracking.
Facilitated dislocation motion at SCCP interfaces preserves flexibility and ductility.
After ion irradiation, the treated alloy will maintain or improve yield strength and ductility relative to the untreated baseline.
Ion irradiation at approximately 800°C is representative of plasma-facing conditions relevant to the proposed effect.
Prolonged exposure or higher temperatures may coarsen the nanoprecipitates.
Nanoprecipitate coarsening would compromise defect-sink behavior and reduce recombination efficiency.
Radiation damage accumulation in an HEA can be retarded by enhanced defect recombination and delayed defect-cluster growth.

The hypothesis is falsified if treated samples show no statistically significant reduction in defect-cluster or void density, or if their post-irradiation mechanical properties are degraded relative to untreated controls.
